## Scope and development status

This plan adopts the final 90-minute programme below. The first 35 minutes
introduce the reproducible research lifecycle through short conceptual
segments, demonstrations, and a two-minute Git activity. The next 40 minutes
are one continuous hands-on
exercise with `targets` and Quarto. `synthpop` is a supplementary exercise
in the workbook, mentioned briefly in the archiving segment. Installation,
production model deployment, and a full treatment of differential privacy
are outside the timed programme.

The [page plan](workshop_pages.qmd) tracks one lesson per programme segment,
the preparation page, and the supplementary exercise. The exercise templates
and reference solutions have been run in the published workshop image under
R 4.4.1. Human review and a timed rehearsal are pending. The lockfile records
the workshop packages under R 4.4.1, with renv 1.0.7.

Participants should have basic familiarity with R and open the prepared
MyBinder environment before the session. The intended result is one
documented workflow with a versioned input, a tracked analysis, a reproducible
report, and a prepared archive record.

## Main learning outcome

Participants should understand and experience an end-to-end reproducible
research workflow. Mastering every individual package is not the aim.

By the end of the programme, participants should be able to:

- Explain how the tools support different parts of a reproducible research workflow.
- Use FAIR principles to document variables, provenance, licensing, and access
  conditions, and interpret an automated assessment.
- Explain how `pins` and `vetiver` link results to specific data and model versions.
- Complete and run a `targets` pipeline and render a Quarto report from its outputs.
- Change an analysis setting, rebuild only what is affected, and reproduce the result.
- Identify the files and metadata needed for a citable release and archive.

The balance suits an interdisciplinary audience. Participants encounter the
complete reproducible research lifecycle while gaining practical experience
with `targets` and Quarto.

## Foundations for the exercises

1. **One dataset throughout.** Use `HealthWellbeing` from section 4.2.4 of
   *Doing Meta-Analysis with R*. A separate pipeline branch trains a small
   regression of Fisher z on log sample size and pins it with `vetiver`.
   The regression and the meta-analysis use the same checked data.
2. **One continuous hands-on exercise.** Provide a partially completed
   `targets` pipeline and Quarto report, so participants modify and execute
   the workflow rather than build everything from scratch. The templates in
   `pipelines/exercise/` each have short TODOs. Participants copy them to the
   ignored `workspace/` folder. The completed references in `pipelines/` serve
   as solutions. Recovery restores the full-dataset REML pipeline and keeps
   participants' report edits so they can complete the Quarto exercise.
3. **One prepared computational environment.** Use MyBinder to provide the
   required packages, configuration, and data. Avoid live installations
   during the workshop. The repository includes the verified raw file, and
   `pipelines/prepare_health_wellbeing.R` prepares the versioned dataset
   inputs before the session.

## Delivery and pacing

- **0–10 minutes, conceptual and hands-on:** introduce the research question, the unit of
  observation, and the principles of understanding, rerunning, auditing,
  tracing, reusing, and citing work. Show the programme as one workflow.
  In the MyBinder Terminal, participants list the public repository's tags,
  read its recent history, and compare their copy of the pipeline with the
  latest commit by its Git hash. The instructor then shows a pull request and
  the releases page on GitHub. Committing and pushing with a fork is follow-up
  material.
- **10–20 minutes, demonstration:** inspect the running R version and the
  lockfile. Explain R package dependencies and the wider computing
  environment. Trace the Dockerfile through GitHub Actions to the MyBinder
  session participants are already using, and save a session record.
- **20–28 minutes, demonstration:** tell participants to watch rather than
  run code. Show how FAIR principles apply to the teaching snapshot. Generate
  JSON-LD from prepared `dataspice` CSVs and show an excerpt that includes
  `n`. Run the `rfair` comparison live on the same file, first from its
  download URL and then with the repository's JSON-LD supplied through
  jsDelivr. Ask the room why the access check fails although the download
  works. Lead from the access statement to identifying the exact dataset
  version. Checking an unpublished record is follow-up material.
- **28–35 minutes, demonstration:** show the two prepared dataset versions on
  a versioned local `pins` board and retrieve each by its identifier. Before
  class, run `source("pipelines/prepare_versioning_demo.R")` in the
  instructor's session. During the demo, use the saved identifier to
  retrieve the model pin and inspect its input prototype, training version,
  and training checksum.
- **35–50 minutes, hands-on:** introduce the pipeline as four stages, select
  input, check studies, fit the meta-analysis, and write the summary, with the
  model pin as a second output from the checked studies. Participants copy the
  partially completed pipeline, run it to see where it stops, and complete two TODOs that create
  missing dependencies. They inspect the graph, build the targets, and rerun
  to see that every target is skipped.
- **50–65 minutes, hands-on:** participants copy and render the partially
  completed report. After definitions of the confidence and prediction
  intervals, they add the confidence interval with inline R, an
  interpretation of the prediction interval, and the provenance fields, and check the rendered values
  against the pipeline summary.
- **65–75 minutes, hands-on:** participants rebuild everything from the
  pinned input and confirm an identical summary. They switch the estimator
  from REML to DL, predict the selective rebuild, and rerender the report.
  Changing the selected dataset version is an optional comparison that
  updates both model branches.
- **75–82 minutes, conceptual:** ask what a colleague would need to rerun the
  report participants just rendered, and build the archive checklist from its
  provenance. Then explain GitHub releases and the release-triggered image
  builds. Show the Zenodo record as an example of how an archive exposes those
  materials through a concept DOI that cites all versions and resolves to the
  latest one. This answers the FAIR question about finding metadata from an
  identifier. Briefly mention `synthpop` for data that cannot be shared, and
  point to the supplementary exercise.
- **82–90 minutes, interactive:** recap what each stage recorded, discuss
  barriers to reproducibility in participants' own work, take questions, and
  remind participants to export their work, summary, and provenance records.

Each hands-on step lists a time allocation, an expected-result checkpoint, and
a collapsed solution. The recovery script selects the full dataset, backs
up the working pipeline, and runs the reference pipeline. Keep the discussion even if
earlier segments overrun. Dates, venues, and announced session details belong
in [announcements](../ANNOUNCEMENTS.md).

## One practical research project

Use the publicly accessible `HealthWellbeing` teaching dataset and pool the
study correlations. Preserve the raw file and explain cleaning, missing-value
checks, and modelling assumptions. Retain the upstream MIT notice when archiving the bundled teaching
snapshot.
[Section 4.2.4, Correlations](https://doing-meta.guide/pooling-es#correlations)

1. **Track the project and environment.** Provide a public Git repository
   containing the pipeline, report, metadata templates, a lockfile, and Docker
   configuration. Participants work in a prepared MyBinder session built from
   it, which has no Git history, and read the repository's history from there.
2. **Document and assess the dataset.** Use `dataspice` to describe the source,
   creators, licence, access conditions, and variables in JSON-LD. Use `rfair`
   to inspect machine-detectable evidence for the teaching snapshot, first
   via the download URL and then with the metadata supplied directly.
3. **Store and retrieve versions.** Store two dataset versions on a local `pins`
   board with versioning enabled explicitly, and retrieve a specified version.
   Retrieve the `vetiver` model pin and match its training version and
   checksum to the inputs of the analysis.
4. **Run the analytical pipeline.** Complete a partially prepared `targets`
   pipeline that connects the selected dataset version, checks, a
   random-effects correlation meta-analysis, and a summary file. The version
   identifier is an explicit input rather than whichever version is newest.
5. **Report the results.** Complete a partially prepared Quarto report that
   reads the summary and records the dataset version, script checksum,
   analytical settings, and software versions needed to trace each result.
6. **Modify and reproduce.** Rebuild from the pinned input, change the estimator,
   and observe which targets and report values change.
7. **Prepare an archive.** Connect a GitHub release to a Zenodo deposit, and
   identify the code, documentation, permitted data, and report it should
   contain. Inspect authorship, licensing, version information, and the
   persistent identifier.

## Tools and scope

| Tool | Planned teaching role | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [R](https://www.r-project.org/) | Shared language and prepared project | Throughout |
| [Git](https://git-scm.com/), [GitHub](https://github.com/) | Change history, collaboration, and sharing | Conceptual, with a two-minute hands-on activity, within the first 10 minutes |
| [renv](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/), [Docker](https://www.docker.com/), [Binder](https://mybinder.org/) | R dependencies, the wider computing environment, and the prepared participant session | Demonstration, 10 minutes; setup completed beforehand |
| [dataspice](https://docs.ropensci.org/dataspice/) | Dataset documentation from prepared CSV files | Demonstration, shared 8 minutes |
| [rfair](https://cran.r-project.org/package=rfair) | Automated FAIR assessment and its limits | Live demonstration, shared 8 minutes |
| [pins](https://pins.rstudio.com/articles/pins.html) | Dataset storage, version identifiers, and historical retrieval | Demonstration, shared 7 minutes; pipeline input in the hands-on exercise |
| [vetiver](https://vetiver.posit.co/get-started/version.html) | Model storage, input prototypes, and training data version | Demonstration, shared 7 minutes; supplementary predictive model |
| [targets](https://docs.ropensci.org/targets/) | Analysis dependencies, tracked outputs, and selective rebuilding | Hands-on, 15 minutes, and 10 minutes modifying and reproducing |
| [Quarto](https://quarto.org/) | Reproducible reporting and publishing | Hands-on, 15 minutes, and rerendering after the modification |
| GitHub releases, [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/) | Releases, archiving, and persistent identifiers | Conceptual, 7 minutes |
| [synthpop](https://www.synthpop.org.uk/) | Synthetic-data illustration and limits on interpretation and sharing | Brief mention; supplementary exercise in the workbook |

`pins` and `vetiver` support versioned storage, but project-specific provenance
links still need to be supplied as metadata. Enable versioning explicitly for a
local folder board. Capture the computational package environment with `renv`
alongside the model's prediction dependencies.

## Supplementary synthpop exercise and responsible sharing

The supplementary exercise uses the full pinned dataset. It generates synthetic
study summaries with CART and seed 123, compares their distributions with the
original, and runs the same pooled analysis on both tables. A runnable
synthetic-data workflow does not let others verify findings computed from
inaccessible originals. Ordinary synthesis with `synthpop` must not be
presented as a differential privacy guarantee; utility or disclosure-risk
scores do not establish one.

Versioning and metadata do not automatically make a dataset or fitted model
appropriate for public release. A model trained on restricted data can reveal
sensitive information, and synthetic data does not confer privacy protection
on related models, evaluation results, or metadata.

A fuller differential privacy extension, if developed later, needs a separate
review of its mechanism, assumptions, privacy accounting, and randomness before
any guarantee is claimed. It is outside the timed programme.

Background: [NIST's synthetic-data overview](https://www.nist.gov/blogs/cybersecurity-insights/differentially-private-synthetic-data)
and [guidelines for evaluating differential privacy guarantees](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/226/final).
